endorsements.title: Developing, purchasing, implementing and monitoring AI tools in radiology: practical considerations. A multi-society statement
endorsements.issuer: ACR, CAR, ESR, RANZCR, RSNA; Radiol Artif Intell 2024 (PMID 38251899, doi:10.1148/ryai.230513)
endorsements.quote: Thirdly, impressive, or “WOW cases,” should be identified to demonstrate the AI model’s value to users and stakeholders.

endorsements.title: Developing, Purchasing, Implementing and Monitoring AI Tools in Radiology: Practical Considerations. A Multi-Society Statement from the ACR, CAR, ESR, RANZCR and RSNA
endorsements.quote: Thirdly, impressive, or “WOW cases,” should be identified to demonstrate the AI model’s value to users and stakeholders.

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether showcasing clinically impressive cases during local evaluation improves stakeholder buy-in or adoption of beneficial AI tools. The recommendation rests on expert guidance from a single multi-society radiology statement, which appears twice in the source list.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice, and zero studies document the hazard of low buy-in. The two endorsements quote identical text from one ACR, CAR, ESR, RANZCR and RSNA statement, so they count as a single expert opinion. Under GRADE conventions, expert opinion without supporting data does not raise certainty above no direct evidence.

No study measures whether presenting selected impressive cases changes how clinicians weigh AI output. The supplied evidence therefore cannot show whether the practice affects the rate of errors that reach patients, in either direction.

commentary.research_gap: Studies should compare local evaluations that present selected impressive cases with evaluations that report only aggregate performance. Outcomes should include clinician adoption, stakeholder approval decisions, and whether users' trust matches the tool's measured accuracy. No such study appears in the supplied evidence, and no study documents how often low buy-in blocks adoption of beneficial tools.
commentary.underserved_note: No test of the practice exists, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups cannot tell from this evidence whether impressive cases drawn from local data would represent their patients or would influence adoption decisions for them.
